text: Raylan Givens wore the hat like he meant it.
Some men wore a hat to look tough.
Raylan knew trouble's face.
Harlan County had a long memory.
So did Raylan.
He knew the roads, the hollers, the old grudges.
The kind of men who smiled right before they reached for a gun.
Then he went inside.
The room got quieter when Raylan entered.
That was usually a sign.
Raylan kept walking.
The man in the booth talked like a man trying to sound brave.
Raylan let him talk.
That made angry men wild.
The man said Raylan had no business in Harlan.
He said old matters should stay buried.
He said men with badges did not understand how things worked there.
Raylan nodded a little, like he was hearing weather.
The man's gun hit the floor before the man had finished his mistake.
Nobody spoke.
Raylan kicked the gun away and looked down at the man in the booth.
Some men would ignore it.
They came for Raylan on a back road.
That was not creative, but it was honest.
It was going to be that kind of night.
He stepped out slowly, because fast movement made things stupid faster.
The men spread out.
One of them shouted for him to drop his gun.
Raylan looked at the road, then at the ditch, then at the men.
Raylan kept his gun trained and called out, "Hands where I can see them." This time, they listened.
The road went quiet except for engines and heavy breathing.
Raylan walked forward and cleared the weapons one by one.
The real trouble was still ahead.
The final man wanted a showdown.
Some men did.
A showdown was usually just a bad choice with witnesses.
They met in an old coal yard as the light came up.
Rusted metal stood around them.
Gravel crunched under Raylan's boots.
The other man stood with his coat open and his hand close.
The shot cracked once, and the fight was over.
The man hit the gravel and did not get back up.
Raylan stood still a moment, gun low, eyes steady.
Justice was still wearing the hat.
